_meta.schema: DESIGN.md section 10.2-10.3. Every option writes into channels the engine already understands.
_meta.note: Costs are % of GDP per year unless stated. reformIndex is 0-100 and feeds the reform stock. Political fit is -1..+1 per party and drives the House vote (POLITICS.md).
_meta.sources: See RESEARCH note in POLICIES.md. Figures are from reporting current to August 2026 and should be re-checked before publication.
_meta.flags: Options may declare `requires` (flags that must be set for the card to appear), `sets` and `clears`. This is what makes cancellation prune a branch and open another - DESIGN.md section 10.3. Flags set at scenario start represent the February 2026 inheritance.
_meta.dependsOn: An option may declare dependsOn: {flag, withoutFactor, note}. If the flag is not set, the option's effects are scaled by withoutFactor. This is how one reform becomes the precondition for another actually working, rather than merely being described that way in the briefing.
_meta.requiresFlags: An option may declare requiresFlags: [...] — a HARD prerequisite. The option is shown locked until every flag is set. Distinct from dependsOn, which is a soft discount. Together these form the tech tree: Digital Government -> Civil Service Reform; Super Licence -> OECD accession; VAT Reform -> Negative Income Tax.

policies.name: Super Licence and Omnibus Law
policies.briefing: Replace ministry-by-ministry approvals with one unified licence and consolidate up to 7,000 overlapping business rules. Target: super licence live within 180 days, full omnibus within a year. Almost no fiscal cost. The slowest approving agencies lose their veto, so they resist.

options.label: Full omnibus consolidation
options.flavour: The cheapest real reform going. Costs almost nothing. Almost nobody in your coalition wants it.

dependsOn.note: A unified licence is meaningless if ministries cannot see each other's records. Without whole-of-government digital migration the omnibus delivers barely half its effect.

options.label: Super licence only, defer the omnibus
options.flavour: Half the reform, a third of the enemies.

options.label: Take no action
options.flavour: Seven thousand overlapping rules stay where they are. The ministries that wrote them are relieved.

policies.name: OECD Accession
policies.briefing: Thailand submitted its Initial Memorandum in December 2025 and is in technical review. Accession means alignment on competition policy, state enterprise governance, anti-corruption, investment openness and corporate governance. The most demanding reform programme on offer. Almost no fiscal cost. Nothing delivers inside one term.

options.label: Accelerate the roadmap
options.flavour: Every chapter is a fight with a ministry that likes things as they are. Payoff in the 2030s.
options.lockedNote: Requires the Super Licence. OECD investment-openness chapters cannot be met while approvals still run ministry by ministry.

options.label: Proceed at technical pace
options.flavour: Progress reports, working groups, no confrontations.

options.label: Let it drift
options.flavour: The working groups continue. The chapters do not. Nobody says it out loud.

policies.name: Civil Service Reform
policies.briefing: 1.8 million core civil servants, 3.0 million with teachers, medics, police and military. Personnel and pensions cost about 1.4 trillion baht, near a third of spending; the Budget Office wants a 35% cap by 2032. Plan: cut the core to 1.35 million via voluntary early retirement for 414,000 officials around 40, from fiscal 2027. Severance now, savings over a decade.

options.label: Full early-retirement programme

lag.note: severance now, wage bill relief from 2029

options.flavour: You are asking the bureaucracy to vote for its own reduction. It will resist, and it implements everything else.
options.lockedNote: Requires Digital Government. The state cannot shed a third of its staff until something automates their work.

options.label: Freeze hiring, let attrition do it
options.flavour: Slower, cheaper, survivable. About a decade to do what the full scheme does in four years.

options.label: Leave the establishment alone
options.flavour: A third of the budget, untouched, growing.

policies.name: Ministry Restructure — Tourism, Culture and Sport
policies.briefing: The Public Sector Development Commission wants sport split into its own ministry and the rest merged into a Ministry of Culture and Tourism. The case is soft power. The cost is eighteen months of senior attention for an org chart. Tourism was 2.7 trillion baht in 2025; arrivals fell 7.2% waiting for China to come back.

options.label: Split sport out and merge tourism with culture
options.flavour: Two new permanent secretaries and eighteen months of fighting over budget lines. Real soft-power gains, real disruption.

options.label: Create the sports ministry, leave tourism where it is
options.flavour: The half with a constituency. Sport gets its own budget; tourism keeps its letterhead.

options.label: Leave the machinery alone
options.flavour: Reorganising ministries is what governments do when they have no policy.

policies.name: Party Finance and Organisation Act
policies.briefing: The networks are gone and the party still has to fight an election. The Party Development Fund shared 117 million baht across 77 parties in 2020. Its formula (votes 40%, dues 40%, branches 20%) is gamed with paper branches and ghost members. Enforce it and money moves from machines to organisations. You have no machine left.

options.label: Enforce the formula, audit the branches, fund against projects
options.flavour: Audited dues and branches decide the money, paid against projects, constituency spending capped. The existing law, enforced. Two thirty-family parties in this parliament lose.

options.label: Enlarge the fund, leave the formula alone
options.flavour: More money, same formula, every party happy. The ghost branches draw a bigger subsidy.

options.label: Not this parliament
options.flavour: The party gave up patronage finance and has nothing in its place. That does not last.

policies.name: Negative Income Tax
policies.briefing: Replace the subsidy patchwork with one income-tested transfer from 2027, threshold around 60,000 baht a year. Only 10 million of 67 million Thais file, so it means mass enrolment into the tax net. The Finance Ministry pairs it with a VAT rise above 7%.

options.label: Implement, funded from general revenue
options.flavour: Makes 20 million people file for the first time. They will notice. Proper funding means the VAT card.
options.lockedNote: Requires VAT Reform or the Revenue Mobilisation Package. Revenue flat at 21% of GDP cannot fund transfers to twenty million new filers.

options.label: Transfers without the VAT rise
options.flavour: All of the cost, none of the funding. Popular. Debt is already at the 70% ceiling.

dependsOn.note: Unfunded by design — the debt does the funding.

options.label: Defer to the next government
options.flavour: Everyone agrees it should happen. Just not now.

policies.name: Thai Chuay Thai Plus
policies.briefing: Co-payment stimulus: 1,000 baht a month for four months to about 30 million Thais aged 18+, spendable only within the month. About 120 billion baht, 0.63% of GDP. Transfer multiplier 0.30, the weakest tool available, and with household debt at 87.5% much goes on repayments.

options.label: Run the full scheme
options.flavour: Everyone gets a thousand baht and remembers who gave it. Four months of goodwill, nothing else.

options.label: Means-test to the bottom 40%
options.flavour: Twice the multiplier per baht, a fraction of the gratitude.

options.label: Redirect the funds to public investment
options.flavour: Done once before: 157 billion baht moved out of the Digital Wallet. Multiplier 0.30 becomes 0.675. Nobody thanks you.

policies.name: Thailand Individual Savings Account (TISA)
policies.briefing: Tax-advantaged accounts for Thai equities, approved December 2025. Deduction up to 800,000 baht; earners under 1.5 million baht may deduct 1.3 times their contribution. Targets about 11.4 million earners. Deepens the capital market and props up the SET, but only the 10 million who file benefit.

options.label: Launch as approved
options.flavour: Deepens the capital market. The benefit goes to people who already file.

options.label: Equalise deduction rights across income bands
options.flavour: Fairer, pricier, and the brokerages stop returning your calls.

options.label: Shelve it
options.flavour: The capital market stays shallow. The 11.4 million who file keep their money in deposits.

policies.name: VAT Reform
policies.briefing: VAT has sat at 7% for three decades against a statutory 10%. Finance's path: 8.5% in 2028, 10% in 2030, plus 1 baht/litre fuel excise from 2027, for revenue of 15.1% of GDP and a sub-3% deficit by FY2029. Each point is about 0.55% of GDP. Tax multiplier -1.125, the largest. The Revenue Mobilisation Package raises about two-thirds as much.

options.label: Keep VAT at 7%
options.flavour: The thirty-fourth consecutive year of the temporary reduction.

options.label: Phased: 8.5% in 2028, 10% in 2030
options.flavour: The published plan. Half the revenue arrives after the next election.

options.label: Go straight to 10%
options.flavour: Closes the gap in one move and funds everything on the desk. The opposition gets its slogan. -1.65pp of output on impact.

policies.name: Revenue Mobilisation Package
policies.briefing: The half of the Finance Ministry plan nobody campaigns against: 1 baht per litre fuel excise from 2027, higher excise on alcohol, tobacco and vehicles, capped income tax deductions, and, biggest of all, collecting tax already assessed. Only 10 million of 67 million Thais file. Raises less than three VAT points. Nobody takes to the street.

options.label: Full package — excise, deduction caps, collection

dependsOn.note: Most of the yield is better collection, not higher rates — and the Revenue Department cannot collect what it cannot see. Without whole-of-government digital migration this delivers well under two-thirds.

options.flavour: Two-thirds of a phased VAT rise's revenue, a fraction of the fight. Only non-payers notice.

options.label: Fuel and sin excise only
options.flavour: The path of least resistance. Enough to unlock the transfer programme, not enough to fund it comfortably.

options.label: No revenue measure
options.flavour: Revenue stays at 21% of GDP, where it has been for a decade.

policies.name: Central Cooperative Debt Consolidation

proposal.note: A coalition proposal. Kla Tham's price for its fifty-eight seats is the rural credit agenda it was built on.

policies.briefing: 6,092 cooperatives, 11 million members; savings cooperatives hold 2.27–2.7 trillion baht of loans, about 15% of household debt. Only six of 1,369 report to the credit bureau. Salary deduction pays the cooperative before the member eats. Proposal: one central body to restructure farmer and teacher cooperative debt, with mandatory credit-bureau reporting as the price of entry.

options.label: Create the central body, with mandatory credit-bureau reporting
options.flavour: The reporting matters more than the restructuring: 1,363 lenders are lending blind. The boards will fight it; it exposes the rates their dividends come from.

options.label: Leave the cooperatives to the registrar
options.flavour: The Cooperative Promotion Department supervised this sector into 15% of household debt. It will carry on.

policies.name: The People's Bank

proposal.note: A coalition proposal. Kla Tham's price for its fifty-eight seats is the rural credit agenda it was built on.

policies.briefing: A state bank for micro-loans at capped, below-market rates. Household debt is past 86% of GDP and informal lenders keep the poorest from ever paying it down. But Thai state lenders lend to the connected, ration by queue, and leave losses to later governments.

options.label: Charter the bank with capped rates
options.flavour: Ten points of approval and an unpriced contingent liability. It could displace loan sharks. Usually it becomes Krung Thai again.

options.label: Expand the existing state banks' mandate instead
options.flavour: GSB and BAAC already do this, badly. At least their losses are already on the books.

policies.name: Senior Plus 1 — Employment Incentive
policies.briefing: Thailand became an aged society in 2024 and will be super-aged by 2033, with 18.4 million over 60. It grew old before it grew rich. The 200% corporate deduction for workers over 60 is capped at 15,000 baht salaries and 10% of headcount. Senior Plus 1 doubles the ceiling to 30,000. Should the headcount cap go too?

options.label: Double the ceiling to 30,000 baht and lift the headcount cap
options.flavour: Revenue lost now, participation gained for a decade. The headcount cap is what binds: no firm can staff a shift with over-60s.

options.label: Raise the ceiling only, keep the 10% headcount cap
options.flavour: Better pay for the older workers firms already have. No more of them.

policies.name: Senior Plus 2 — Income Tax Relief
policies.briefing: The worker side is untouched. A working Thai over 60 pays full income tax and loses means-tested support, so staying in work barely pays. Senior Plus 2 grants up to a 50% deduction for over-60s earning under 1.5 million baht a year: almost all of them.

options.label: Grant the full 50% deduction under 1.5 million baht
options.flavour: The most expensive of the three, and the one that changes a household's sums. Hidden income starts appearing on returns.

options.label: A limited 25% deduction, reviewed after two years
options.flavour: Half the cost, less than half the effect. Nobody replans their working life around a two-year review.

policies.name: Land Bridge (Chumphon–Ranong)
policies.briefing: The Southern Economic Corridor land bridge. Over one trillion baht; Phase 1 to open 2030, full completion around 2035. Backers promise a shortcut past the Malacca Strait. Critics: about 54 hours against 48 via Malacca, around US$252 more per container, and 73.9% of Thai trade already uses regional routes.

options.label: Push ahead with Phase 1

lag.note: Nothing lands before 2031. Outside the window.

options.flavour: The South gets a decade of construction. You get the bill and none of the ribbon.

dependsOn.note: Without a revenue measure this is pure borrowing against a ceiling already within five points.

options.label: Delay pending review
options.flavour: Keeps the option and the money, and looks prudent. The file comes back in two quarters.

options.label: Cancel outright
options.flavour: Sound arithmetic, expensive politics. A rail-only link becomes the obvious consolation prize.

policies.name: Chumphon–Ranong Rail Link
policies.briefing: With the Land Bridge cancelled, the corridor falls back to a conventional Gulf–Andaman rail link. A fraction of the cost, no need to lure shippers from Malacca, and something for the South after you took the trillion-baht project away.

options.label: Build the rail link
options.flavour: About a third of Land Bridge Phase 1, and it might carry something.

options.label: Commission a feasibility study
options.flavour: The traditional Thai answer to a corridor that does not add up.

options.label: Leave the corridor alone
options.flavour: Two cancellations in the same region. The South will remember.

policies.name: Northeast HSR — Bangkok–Nong Khai (Phase 2)
policies.briefing: Phase 2 of the Thai–Chinese high-speed railway: Nakhon Ratchasima to Nong Khai, 357 km, about US$10.1 billion, due 2030 and linking to the China–Laos line. Phase 1 has already slipped a year. The biggest capital commitment on offer, geopolitically loaded, and due as your term ends. Whoever wins in 2030 cuts the ribbon.

options.label: Fund Phase 2 and accelerate
options.flavour: Isan gets a railway to China. The budget gets a hole until 2033.

dependsOn.note: Without a revenue measure this is pure borrowing against a ceiling already within five points.

options.label: Finish Phase 1, defer Phase 2
options.flavour: Deliver something before promising more. Unfashionable.

options.label: Renegotiate financing terms with Beijing
options.flavour: Better terms, slower delivery, and a call nobody in the ministry wants to make.

policies.name: Eastern HSR — Three-Airport Link
policies.briefing: Don Mueang–Suvarnabhumi–U-Tapao, the spine of the Eastern Economic Corridor. Eight years late, over 21.8 billion baht sunk, 9.8bn of it public. The concession faces a review that can end it: sites never cleanly handed over, the Makkasan drainage channel unresolved, U-Tapao forecasts cut, financing unclosed. Termination means compensating both sides.

options.label: Amend the concession and proceed
options.flavour: Eight years of delay rewarded with better terms. The Democrats will read the file aloud.

options.label: Terminate the concession
options.flavour: Compensation talks, nothing to show for 21.8 billion baht, and every foreign concessionaire rereading their termination clauses.

options.label: Defer the review again
options.flavour: The ninth year.

policies.name: EEC Conventional Rail (post-termination)
policies.briefing: The high-speed concession is dead. Conventional double-track electrified rail to U-Tapao covers most of the freight and commuter case at a fraction of the cost, and can be built within one term. Eight years and 21.8 billion baht bought a lesson.

options.label: Build conventional double-track to U-Tapao
options.flavour: Finished inside your term. Nobody makes a documentary about double-track.

options.label: Re-tender the high-speed line
options.flavour: Same project, new consortium, same drainage channel at Makkasan.

options.label: No replacement
options.flavour: Twenty-one billion baht, eight years, an empty corridor. The EEC keeps the name.

policies.name: Electric Bus Network
policies.briefing: The BMTA has 150 billion baht of debt, loses 8 billion a year and needs a new fleet. 1,520 electric buses are due by March 2027; Cabinet approved 800 more on lease for 8.14 billion baht and 700 replacing NGV stock for 7.1 billion. Fares stay under a fifth of the minimum wage.

options.label: Full fleet electrification and route overhaul

dependsOn.note: Route rationalisation and integrated ticketing need the data the BMTA does not currently hold.

options.flavour: Visible within two years. Bangkok notices buses; it does not notice the Super Licence.

options.label: Lease the buses, leave the routes alone
options.flavour: New buses, same bad routes. The losses continue.

options.label: Electrify and make it fare-free
options.flavour: The most approval per baht on this desk. It also makes an 8 billion baht annual loss permanent.

policies.name: Small Modular Reactors
policies.briefing: The Power Development Plan includes two 300 MWe small modular reactors, one in the Northeast and one in the South, online in 2037. Thailand has never licensed a power reactor. Capital cost is USD 5,000–10,000 per kW; LCOE USD 90–160/MWh against USD 79–86 for gas. The grid is 60% gas, mostly imported.

options.label: Order both units and build the regulator

dependsOn.note: Vendor selection, fuel supply and the safeguards agreement all run through partners you have not aligned with.

options.flavour: A premium over gas for power in 2037, and a nuclear regulator built from scratch. Neither will win you a vote.

options.label: Order one unit, site it in the Northeast
options.flavour: A demonstration unit. It buys the regulator, the fuel deal and trained inspectors without betting the grid.

options.label: Fund the feasibility and siting study only
options.flavour: Three years of consultants and hearings in every candidate province. The decision passes to the next government.

options.label: Strike the reactors from the plan
options.flavour: Uranium fever has done and got me down / Uranium fever it's spreadin' all around

policies.name: Semiconductor and Advanced Electronics
policies.briefing: Three years of roadmap produced one finding: Thailand cannot buy its way into wafer fabrication. It can reach advanced packaging, test, power devices and design services if it trains the engineers. BOI's draft roadmap cites 2.5 trillion baht of investment over the decade, none of it inside your term.

options.label: Fund the full package — packaging, design centres, 86,000 engineers

dependsOn.note: Without three years of a funded board there is no secretariat, no curriculum and no pipeline to accelerate — the programme starts from a standing start.

options.flavour: Sound use of public money with little to show by December 2030. Your successor reports the numbers.

options.label: Build a national champion around the sovereign programme
options.lockedNote: Requires a sovereign AI course. Without one there is no national champion to build around.
options.flavour: State-directed and domestically owned. Also Alphatec's business plan with a bigger budget, and everyone remembers how that ended.

dependsOn.note: A champion with no domestic AI capacity to serve is a fabrication subsidy looking for a customer — the TH-AI redirect is what gives it demand.

options.label: Leave the sector to the BOI incentives already in place
options.flavour: Assembly and test, priced against Vietnam, for as long as the wage gap holds.

policies.name: TH-AI Passport
policies.briefing: 1.6 billion baht from the Digital Economy fund gives five million Thais aged 15+ a year of access to twelve premium AI models, with mandatory upskilling. Cost: 0.008% of GDP. Critics say it subsidises foreign platforms, breeds passive use and deepens dependence. Contractor selection is under question.

options.label: Run the programme as designed
options.flavour: Costs almost nothing and polls well. The productivity gain arrives after everyone here has retired.

options.label: Redirect toward domestic AI capacity
options.flavour: Builds something Thai instead of renting something American. Slower, and the procurement questions remain.

options.label: Cancel over procurement concerns
options.flavour: The procurement questions were fair. The five million people promised the tools will not read the audit.

policies.name: Digital Government
policies.briefing: The Digital Government Development Agency is moving ministries onto shared cloud: e-Sarabun documents with digital signatures and ThaiID, e-Meeting, and the Government Data Cloud. It is cheap and dull, and both civil service reduction and the Super Licence depend on it.

options.label: Mandate whole-of-government migration
options.flavour: Raises budget execution more than any other card. Every ministry will claim to be a special case.

options.label: Continue voluntary agency onboarding
options.flavour: The agencies that were going to modernise will. The rest will not.

options.label: No additional push
options.flavour: Every ministry keeps its own database, its own signature and its own reason not to share.

policies.name: The 100-Baht Internet Package

proposal.note: A coalition proposal. The Democrats are the smallest party at the table and the only one with an institutional memory of governing.

policies.briefing: Thailand's mobile market is down to two major operators, and prices have risen accordingly. The Democrats propose a mandated 100-baht broadband package for low-income households, delivered through the universal service obligation. It is a price control. It also connects the households your digital services assume are online.

options.label: Mandate the package through the universal service obligation

dependsOn.note: Connectivity is only worth what there is to connect to — without the service migration this is a cheaper bill, not a capability.

options.flavour: Popular, cheap, and it completes your digital push. The operators will sue, and investors will remember.

options.label: Leave it to the regulator
options.flavour: The NBTC has left it to the market since the merger. The market has noticed.

policies.name: Zero Corruption Act

proposal.note: A coalition proposal. The Economic Party holds three seats inside Others and one item of leverage: the FINAL EXIT programme it ran on.

policies.briefing: The Economic Party's ZERO CORRUPTION plank: the death penalty for public corruption, execution within a year of a Supreme Court verdict. Thai law already allows it for serious graft — the 2018 organic act extended it to foreign officials — but it has never been used. This version makes it mandatory. Three coalition seats ran on this.

options.label: Pass the Act as drafted, mandatory execution and all
options.flavour: Do you dare have the gall to do this?

options.label: Take the enforcement, drop the death penalty
options.flavour: The most popular and most dangerous thing on this desk. Real enforcement reaches your own donors, provincial members and vote-deliverers. Institutional support falls because you are prosecuting the establishment.
options.lockedNote: Requires accelerated OECD accession and a civil service already cut. Without both, an anti-corruption body is a new office staffed by the same people.

options.label: Thank them and shelve it
options.flavour: The safe answer. They will remember it at every division. Three seats is not many until the margin is three.

policies.name: Justice System Reform

proposal.note: A coalition proposal. The Economic Party holds three seats inside Others and one item of leverage: the FINAL EXIT programme it ran on.

policies.briefing: The second half of FINAL EXIT: separate arrest from investigation. Today the same police who investigate a case decide who is detained, which lets protection networks turn enforcement into revenue. Every Thai policing review since 2007 has recommended the split. Every one has been blocked.

options.label: Separate investigation from arrest, prosecutors direct the file
options.flavour: This dissolves grey capital. The police have defeated it for twenty years. You lose their cooperation; the informal sector gains a reason to formalise.
options.lockedNote: Requires the Zero Corruption Act with real enforcement. Without a body to prosecute what investigators find, the bottleneck just moves.

options.label: Pilot it in three provinces and review
options.flavour: Pilots have killed this reform three times: it works, the review is set for after the election, and it vanishes.

options.label: Not this parliament
options.flavour: The Royal Thai Police are content, and so is everyone who has ever paid them.

policies.name: Migrant Labour Regularisation
policies.briefing: 3.65 million registered migrant workers, mostly from Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos; 1.4 million have social security. The MOU channel moved from 635,000 to 655,000. The October 2025 e-WorkPermit failure left over a million Myanmar workers at risk. Agency renewals cost tens of thousands of baht against under 4,000 done directly. When 300,000 Cambodians left, the longan harvest lost 2.6 billion baht.

options.label: One-stop regularisation, brokers cut out, social security enrolment mandatory
options.flavour: The biggest formalisation move available, and the most expensive politically. Costs come before contributions, and the brokers are embedded in the ministries that must run it. Expect an ugly whip count and lost approval.

options.label: Widen the MOU channel and leave the rest alone
options.flavour: Doubles a channel carrying a fifth of the workforce. The brokers keep the other four fifths.

options.label: Enforcement first — raids, fines, deportations
options.flavour: Popular, and it drives workers underground, not out. Ask the longan growers what a labour shortage costs.

policies.name: Tourism Workforce Reskilling
policies.briefing: The target is up to 10 million tourism jobs, backed by free upskilling in digital tourism, hospitality standards and AI. It sits in the five-ministry human-capital strategy (Labour, Education, Higher Education, Social Development, Agriculture), which has not been costed. Tourism is the largest employer of non-graduates.

options.label: Fund the full programme with a credit-bank qualification behind it

dependsOn.note: delivered through five ministries that cannot see each other's records

options.flavour: Human capital is the slowest channel, and this is the last quarter to start it. Little return before the election. Without digital government, most of it leaks between five ministries.

options.label: Hospitality standards only, no digital component
options.flavour: The training the industry has always asked for. The workforce stays just as exposed to automation.

options.label: The sector trains its own
options.flavour: It does, informally, on the job, to no standard anybody can put on a CV.

policies.name: High-Value Agriculture

proposal.note: A coalition proposal. Pheu Thai's constituency is agricultural, and it has not had a farm policy of its own since rice pledging.

policies.briefing: About a third of Thai jobs are in agriculture, producing under a tenth of output. The proposal moves the sector up the value chain: precision farming, synthetic biology and biorefining under the BCG national agenda, contract standards for smallholders, and net-zero targets for Europe. Same constituency as rice-pledging, opposite instrument.

options.label: Fund the full transition — precision farming, biorefining, standards

dependsOn.note: Traceability and contract standards run on registries the ministry does not currently hold.

options.flavour: The best farm policy in twenty years, and the slowest. Smallholders need three seasons and credit; you offer one.

options.label: Input subsidies and a price floor instead
options.flavour: Twelve points of approval, and the lesson of 2011 to 2014 discarded to get them.

options.label: Leave the sector to the existing schemes
options.flavour: Thirty per cent of the workforce, eight per cent of output, no plan. Every government's position since 2014.

policies.name: Converting Sor Por Kor Land Deeds

proposal.note: A coalition proposal. Kla Tham's price for its fifty-eight seats is the rural credit agenda it was built on.

policies.briefing: 1.62 million farmers hold 22.07 million rai on Sor Por Kor 4-01 documents: land they may farm but not borrow against. The conversion bill, driven by Thamanat at the agriculture ministry, requires five years' cultivation, limits transfers to eligible farmers, and makes the deed usable as bank collateral. Past reforms ended with ineligible owners.

options.label: Convert the documents to full title deeds
options.flavour: Twenty-two million rai become collateral. Only the transfer restrictions stand between that and a land grab, and they rarely outlast the government that wrote them.

options.label: Leave the documents as they are
options.flavour: Safe. 1.62 million households keep farming land they cannot borrow against.

policies.name: Mental Health in the Universal Scheme

proposal.note: A coalition proposal. Universal coverage is Pheu Thai's founding achievement and it would like a second chapter.

policies.briefing: Thailand has 1.3 psychiatrists per 100,000 people; the global average is 13. About 13.4 million Thais report a mental health condition; 89% got no care last year, 8.2% formal treatment. The Department of Mental Health gets 1.8% of the health budget. The proposal writes mental health into the universal coverage scheme, with a six-year training pipeline.

options.label: Write it into the scheme and fund the training pipeline
options.flavour: Cheap but slow: the psychiatrists you fund qualify after you leave. Untreated illness costs more output than the programme.

options.label: Not in this budget
options.flavour: The Department of Mental Health keeps its 1.8%. Nobody protests; this constituency is not organised.

policies.name: Senior Plus 3 — One Village, One Volunteer Nurse
policies.briefing: Tax relief does nothing for the third of the elderly who cannot work. Thailand's million village health volunteers have a stipend and a fortnight's training. This puts a qualified nurse behind the network in each of some 75,000 villages, doing home visits before emergencies happen.

options.label: Fund the nationwide programme and the training pipeline
options.flavour: The limit is nurses, not money, and nurses take four years. The government after yours delivers it. Nobody will credit you for the admissions avoided.

options.label: Limit it to the twenty oldest provinces
options.flavour: Targets the need. The other fifty-seven provinces read about it in the newspaper.

policies.name: Fully Funded 15-Year Education

proposal.note: A coalition proposal. The Democrats are the smallest party at the table and the only one with an institutional memory of governing.

policies.briefing: Free 15-year schooling has been the Democrats' own policy since 2009. The state pays a per-head subsidy; families pay transport, materials, registration and fees, so households under 2,802 baht a month still drop children out at grades 6-7 and 9-10. The proposal funds the full household cost and reweights toward remote schools.

options.label: Fund it properly — materials, transport, fees, and a remote-school weighting
options.flavour: The highest human-capital return on this desk and the slowest: a child kept in school past grade 9 this year starts work in 2038.

options.label: Keep the existing per-head subsidy
options.flavour: It has been called free for seventeen years. One more will not be noticed by anyone not paying for it.

policies.name: Vulnerable Demographic Allowances

proposal.note: A coalition proposal. Palang Pracharath sits inside Others, is short of a cause, and has always been strongest with the elderly vote.

policies.briefing: The old-age allowance is tiered by age: 600 baht a month at 60, rising to 1,000 only at 90. Thailand will be 'super-aged' within a decade. The proposal: a flat 1,000 baht for everyone over 60 and a wider maternal grant. Popular and permanent.

options.label: Flat 1,000 baht at 60, and widen the maternal grant
options.flavour: Eleven reliable points of approval, and a permanent claim on a budget facing a fast-worsening dependency ratio. Your successors pay too.

options.label: Keep the existing tiers
options.flavour: Fiscally correct, politically friendless. The 600-baht rate has not risen in real terms in over a decade.

policies.name: Provincial Tourism Allocations
policies.briefing: The Tourism Promotion Fund holds 10 billion baht. The proposal gives 100 million to each of the 77 provinces — 7.7 billion —, since foreign arrivals cluster in five provinces. Domestic tourism reached 1.16 trillion baht last year and grew while foreign arrivals fell 4.7%. Mae Hong Son and Chon Buri get the same envelope.

options.label: One hundred million to every province, no conditions
options.flavour: Seventy-seven governors with a budget line and a ribbon. Good politics; economically, close to a plain transfer.

options.label: Allocate against submitted proposals, audited afterwards
options.flavour: Better spending, worse politics. Every province that loses will say the criteria were written in Bangkok.

options.label: Keep the fund centralised
options.flavour: The money keeps going to the five provinces that were always going to be full.
